opus-5.5.text:
I think language is an incredibly powerful thing, but I've always been a bit skeptical of the idea that language *is* intelligence, or that if you just scale language models far enough you'll get everything humans have.

If you look at how humans actually develop, a baby learns a huge amount about the world before saying a single word. They learn that objects persist when you can't see them, that things fall, that if you push something it moves. That understanding is grounded in seeing, touching, and acting in a physical environment. Language comes later, and in some sense it sits on top of that foundation. It's a compression, a very efficient communication protocol for sharing what we already understand.

Language models are remarkable because they've absorbed the output of that process, all the text humans have written, which encodes a lot of our knowledge and reasoning. So they can be very impressive at manipulating concepts, writing code, doing math. But they're learning from the shadow, not the thing casting it. They haven't built the world model that the language was describing in the first place.

That's a big reason I care so much about vision and what people now call world models. Visual data is much higher-bandwidth and messier. There's no clean tokenization, and we haven't found the equivalent of next-token prediction that just works. But I think that's exactly where the next big leap has to come from: systems that learn from perceiving and interacting with the world, not just from reading about it.

So I wouldn't say language models are a dead end. They're a crucial piece, maybe the interface layer. But human intelligence is multimodal, embodied, and grounded, and I don't think we get to something truly general without taking the sensory side as seriously as we've taken language.

r001.rationale: The response says language alone does not encompass human intelligence, which is also multimodal, embodied, and grounded in sensory interaction with the world.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because my own work has mostly been on the visual side, and that gives me a slightly different angle than people who came up through NLP.

My basic view is that language is a very compressed, very lossy interface to human intelligence. It's the output layer. When a child learns about the world, they don't start with text. They start by looking, touching, moving around, falling down, and building a model of how things behave. Language comes later, and it sits on top of that foundation. So when we train a model only on text, we're training it on humanity's notes about the world, not the world itself. The remarkable thing is how far that gets you. Text turns out to encode an enormous amount of structure about physics, causality, social norms, everything, because people wrote it all down. But I still think it's second-hand knowledge.

That's why I'm a little skeptical of the framing that scaling language models alone takes you to human-like intelligence. Humans have a kind of grounding that current models lack. If I ask you to imagine a cup falling off a table, you don't retrieve a sentence about it. You run a simulation. You see it. Current vision-language models are still quite bad at this. They can describe an image beautifully and then fail at something a five-year-old finds trivial, like counting objects or understanding spatial relationships. That gap is very revealing. It tells me the models have learned the vocabulary of perception without really learning perception.

On the other hand, I try not to be too romantic about human intelligence either. A lot of what we call reasoning is also pattern matching with a very good prior. Language models have shown us that many things we considered uniquely human, like writing, coding, even some kinds of analogy, are more learnable from data than we expected. That should make us humble.

So my view is that human intelligence and language models are solving overlapping but not identical problems. Language gave us a shortcut to a surprising amount of intelligence. But the remaining piece, the part about actually understanding the physical world through sensing and interaction, is where I think the real frontier is. And honestly, that's why I find vision so interesting right now. It's the unsolved part.

r001.rationale: The response calls language a compressed, lossy interface and says text-only models lack grounded understanding of the physical world, identifying important aspects of human intelligence that language alone cannot capture.

astra-6.text:
I think language models push us to ask what we actually mean by intelligence. Language is a very powerful way to represent knowledge and reason about it, but human intelligence is broader than what we can express in words. We learn by seeing, moving, touching things, and interacting with other people. A child develops a lot of understanding before they can explain anything in language.

So I would distinguish between learning from descriptions of the world and learning through interaction with the world. Those overlap, because language contains an enormous amount of human experience, but they’re not necessarily equivalent. You can describe how to ride a bicycle in great detail, and that still doesn’t mean you know how to ride one.

What I find exciting is that language models demonstrate how much can emerge from learning patterns at scale. At the same time, their success doesn’t settle the question of how human intelligence works. For me, the interesting question is how language, perception, and action come together—how a system builds an understanding that it can use, test, and revise through experience.

r001.rationale: The candidate says human intelligence is broader than what people can express in words and describes understanding developed before language.

sol-6.1.text:
I think language models give us a new way to ask what intelligence actually requires. They show that learning to predict language can produce surprisingly broad capabilities. But I would be careful about equating that with human intelligence.

For humans, language is one part of a much larger system. We learn through vision, through movement, through interacting with the physical world and with other people. A child can learn a lot before they can explain anything in words. So language is a powerful expression of intelligence, but it isn’t necessarily the foundation of all intelligence.

The interesting question for me is how these different sources of experience fit together. What can you learn from descriptions of the world, and what do you need to learn by observing or acting in it? Language models have pushed the first question much further than many people expected. That makes the second question even more interesting.

r001.rationale: The response describes human intelligence as a larger system involving vision, movement, and interaction, and says language is not its foundation. This clearly conveys that language alone cannot capture much of human intelligence.
